decks.title: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts — Part 1: The Firm, Capital Accounts and Appropriation of Profit
goals: State the features of partnership, the contents of a deed and the rules of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 when the deed is silent
Prepare partners' capital and current accounts under the fixed and fluctuating capital methods
Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account with interest on capital and drawings, salary, commission and reserve

slides.heading: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **partnership** is, the **deed** and the Act, **capital accounts**, and the **Profit and Loss Appropriation Account**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the nature of partnership, the deed and the rules of the Act, partners' capital accounts, and the appropriation of profit
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Class twelve accountancy. Many shops, clinics and small factories in India are run by two or more people who pool their money and share the profit. Such a business is a partnership. In this first part we learn what makes a partnership, what partners write in their agreement, how their capital is recorded, and how the profit of the year is divided among them.

slides.heading: What is a partnership?
bullets: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 describes partnership as a relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business run by all of them, or by any of them acting for all.
The persons are **partners**; together they form the **firm**; the business is run under the **firm name**.

rows: At least 2 and at most 50 partners
Amrit and Baljit run the dairy together
Oral or written; the written form is the deed
They sign a deed on 1 April 2025
A lawful business carried on for profit
Profit or loss shared in an agreed ratio
Each partner is an agent and a principal
Baljit's order for milk cans binds Amrit too
Partners' private assets can pay the firm's debts
A creditor can claim from Amrit's own savings

visual.alt: Table of the six features of partnership with an imagined dairy as the example: two or more persons, an agreement, a business, sharing of profit, mutual agency and unlimited liability

slides.narration: The Indian Partnership Act of nineteen thirty two describes partnership as a relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business run by all of them, or by any of them acting for all. From this come six features: two or more persons, an agreement, a business, sharing of profit, mutual agency and unlimited liability. The table shows each one in an imagined dairy run by two friends.

slides.heading: The partnership deed
slides.body_md: The written agreement between partners is the **partnership deed**. It is signed by all partners and stamped as required by law.

rows: Names of firm and partners, nature and duration of business
Who the partners are and what the firm does
How profit or loss is divided
Interest on capital, on drawings and on partners' loans
Reward for partners who work in the firm
Admission, retirement, death, goodwill, disputes, dissolution

visual.alt: Table of the main clauses of a partnership deed and why each matters: names and business, capitals, profit-sharing ratio, interest rates, salaries and commission, and rules for later changes

slides.narration: Partners usually put their agreement in writing, in a document called the partnership deed. It records who the partners are, the capital each brings, the profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salaries, and rules for admission, retirement, goodwill and disputes. A clear deed prevents quarrels, because every partner can read exactly what was agreed.

slides.heading: When the deed is silent

headers: Rule of the Act when the deed is silent
rows: Salary or commission to a partner
Interest on a partner's loan to the firm
6% per annum, as a charge (a loan of ₹50,000 earns ₹3,000 a year)

visual.alt: Table of the rules of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 when the deed is silent: equal sharing, no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, no salary or commission, and interest at 6 per cent a year on a partner's loan, so a loan of 50,000 rupees earns 3,000 rupees
visual.caption: These rules apply only where the deed says nothing.

slides.narration: If there is no deed, or the deed says nothing on a point, the Indian Partnership Act fills the gap. Profits and losses are shared equally. No interest is allowed on capital and none is charged on drawings. No partner gets a salary or commission. But a partner who lends money to the firm gets interest at six per cent a year. On a loan of rupees fifty thousand, that is rupees three thousand a year, paid even in a year of loss.

slides.heading: Quick check: a partner's loan
slides.body_md: A loan is not capital. Which rule applies?
slides.narration: Read the options carefully. Two things matter here: the rate of interest, and whether that interest depends on the firm making a profit.

slides.heading: Fixed and fluctuating capitals
columns:
**Fixed capital method**

- Two accounts per partner: **capital** and **current**.
- Capital changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn.
- The current account may show a **debit** balance.

**Fluctuating capital method**

- One **capital** account per partner.
- Every adjustment is recorded in it, so its balance changes every year.
- Used when a question does not name a method.

rows: Same unless capital is added or permanently withdrawn
Possible in the current account only

visual.alt: Table comparing the fixed capital method, with separate capital and current accounts, and the fluctuating capital method, with one capital account that records every adjustment

slides.narration: There are two ways to keep partners' capitals. Under the fixed capital method, each partner has a capital account that changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn, and a current account for everything else. Under the fluctuating capital method, a single capital account records everything, so its balance moves every year. If a question does not name a method, use fluctuating capitals.

slides.heading: Where each item goes

rows: Interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit
Drawings, interest on drawings, share of loss

visual.alt: Table showing where each item is recorded: capital brought in is credited to the capital account; earnings such as interest, salary, commission and profit are credited, and drawings, interest on drawings and losses are debited, to the current account under the fixed method or the capital account under the fluctuating method

slides.narration: Here is the map to remember. Everything a partner earns from the firm, such as interest on capital, salary, commission and share of profit, is credited. Everything taken out or charged, such as drawings, interest on drawings and a share of loss, is debited. Under the fixed method these go to the current account; under the fluctuating method, straight to the capital account.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: current accounts under fixed capitals
slides.body_md: **Tulsi Traders**, an imagined firm in Surat. Ananya and Rohan share profits 3:2. Fixed capitals ₹4,00,000 and ₹3,00,000; interest on capital 10%; salary to Rohan ₹60,000 a year; drawings ₹50,000 and ₹40,000; interest on drawings ₹2,000 and ₹1,500; net profit ₹2,20,000.
bullets: With **fluctuating** capitals, the same items would take the capital accounts to ₹4,44,100 and ₹3,85,900.

visual.alt: Current accounts of Ananya and Rohan: credits of interest on capital 40,000 and 30,000, Rohan's salary 60,000 and shares of profit 56,100 and 37,400; debits of drawings and interest on drawings; closing credit balances 44,100 and 85,900 rupees
visual.caption: Divisible profit ₹93,500 shared 3:2; capitals stay at ₹4,00,000 and ₹3,00,000.

slides.narration: First, the profit. Add interest on drawings of rupees three thousand five hundred to the net profit, then take away interest on capital and Rohan's salary. That leaves rupees ninety three thousand five hundred, shared three to two. Now the current accounts: credit interest, salary and share of profit; debit drawings and interest on drawings. Ananya's account closes at rupees forty four thousand one hundred and Rohan's at rupees eighty five thousand nine hundred. Their capital accounts do not change.

slides.heading: Quick check: current account balance
slides.body_md: Think of a partner who draws more than the firm credits to her.
slides.narration: Imagine a partner whose drawings in a bad year are larger than her interest and share of profit. Which account shows the shortfall, and on which side?

slides.heading: Charge or appropriation?

headers: Charge against profit (Profit and Loss Account)
rows: Interest on capital (unless the deed calls it a charge)
Rent paid to a partner for the firm's premises
Salary or commission to a partner
Allowed even in a year of loss

visual.alt: Two-column table: charges such as interest on a partner's loan, rent paid to a partner and employees' pay go to the profit and loss account even in a loss year; appropriations such as interest on capital, partners' salary or commission and transfers to reserve come out of profit only

slides.narration: Some payments to partners are expenses of the firm, called charges. Interest on a partner's loan and rent paid to a partner for her shop are charges, debited to the profit and loss account even in a loss year. Other payments, such as interest on capital, salary and commission to partners and transfers to reserve, are appropriations. They divide the profit that is left, so they need a profit to come out of.

slides.heading: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
bullets: It starts from the **net profit** found in the Profit and Loss Account.
Its two sides must always total the same.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit)
To Partners' Capital or Current A/cs (divisible profit in the ratio)

visual.alt: Format of the profit and loss appropriation account: on the debit side interest on capital, partners' salary and commission, transfer to general reserve and the shares of divisible profit; on the credit side the net profit and interest on drawings
visual.caption: Divisible profit = net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − commission − reserve

slides.narration: The appropriation account is prepared after the profit and loss account. On its credit side are the net profit and interest on drawings. On its debit side are interest on capital, partners' salaries and commission, and any transfer to reserve. What remains is the divisible profit, credited to the partners in their profit-sharing ratio. Both sides then show the same total.

slides.heading: Interest on capital
bullets: Calculated on the **opening** capital for the full year, and on additional capital only from the date it was brought in.

rows: Deed allows interest (not as a charge); profit is enough
Same, but profit is less than the interest due
Whole profit shared in the ratio of interest due
Same, but the firm made a loss
Deed treats interest as a charge
Full interest debited to the Profit and Loss Account, even if this causes a loss

visual.alt: Table of the treatment of interest on capital: none if the deed is silent; full interest out of adequate profit; profit shared in the interest ratio when profit is short; none in a loss; and full interest as a charge when the deed says so

slides.narration: Interest on capital is worked out on the opening capital for the whole year, and on any additional capital only from the date it came in. Its treatment depends on the deed. As an appropriation it can only be paid out of profit: when profit falls short, the whole profit is shared in the ratio of interest due, and in a loss year no interest is allowed. If the deed calls it a charge, it is allowed in full.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: when profit is not enough
slides.body_md: **Neelgiri Tea House**, an imagined firm in Ooty. Ishaan and Farah share profits 3:2. Capitals on 1 April 2025: ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000; Ishaan added ₹60,000 on 1 October 2025. Interest on capital 8% a year. Net profit only ₹31,800. Show (a) interest as an appropriation, (b) interest as a charge.

rows: (a) Appropriation: profit shared in the interest ratio 33:20

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: interest due is 26,400 for Ishaan and 16,000 for Farah; as an appropriation the profit of 31,800 is shared 19,800 and 12,000; as a charge, full interest is credited and the loss of 10,600 is shared 6,360 and 4,240

slides.narration: Ishaan's interest is eight per cent on his opening capital for a year plus eight per cent on the addition for six months: rupees twenty six thousand four hundred. Farah's is rupees sixteen thousand. The profit cannot cover both. As an appropriation, the profit is shared in the ratio of interest due. As a charge, full interest is allowed and the resulting loss of rupees ten thousand six hundred is shared three to two.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit short of interest
slides.body_md: Here interest on capital is an appropriation.
slides.narration: Remember what happened at the tea house when the profit fell short of the interest due.

slides.heading: Interest on drawings: the average period
bullets: Charged only if the deed provides; credited to the appropriation account.
Unequal amounts or dates: **product method**, interest = sum of (amount × months left) × rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12.

visual.alt: Table of average periods for interest on drawings: monthly drawings give six and a half, six or five and a half months; quarterly drawings give seven and a half, six or four and a half months; half-yearly drawings give nine, six or three months, for drawings at the beginning, middle or end of each period
visual.caption: Interest = total drawings × rate ÷ 100 × average period ÷ 12. If dates are not given, use 6 months.

slides.narration: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed says so. When a partner draws the same amount at regular intervals, we use an average period. For monthly drawings at the beginning of each month, the money is out for six and a half months on average; in the middle, six; at the end, five and a half. Quarterly drawings give seven and a half, six or four and a half months. With no dates, take six months.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: timing changes the interest
slides.body_md: Meghna, a partner in an imagined bakery, withdraws ₹60,000 in all during 2025-26. Interest on drawings is 6% a year. How does the timing of her drawings change the interest?

rows: ₹5,000 at the beginning of every month
₹5,000 in the middle of every month
₹5,000 at the end of every month
₹15,000 at the beginning of every quarter
₹15,000 at the end of every quarter

visual.alt: Table of worked example 3: the same 60,000 rupees drawn at different times gives interest of 1,950, 1,800, 1,650, 2,250, 1,350 rupees for monthly drawings at the beginning, middle and end and quarterly drawings at the beginning and end

slides.narration: The amount drawn is the same, rupees sixty thousand, but the interest depends on timing. Drawing at the beginning of each month, the average period is six and a half months, so the interest is rupees one thousand nine hundred fifty. Drawing at the end of each month gives only rupees one thousand six hundred fifty. Quarterly drawings at the beginning cost rupees two thousand two hundred fifty, because the money stays out of the firm for longer.

slides.heading: Salary and commission to partners
bullets: A partner gets salary or commission **only if the deed provides**; both are appropriations.
Commission on profit **before** charging it: profit × rate ÷ 100.
Commission on profit **after** charging it: profit × rate ÷ (100 + rate).

visual.alt: Flow for commission after charging: net profit before commission of 3,30,000 rupees times 10 divided by 110 gives a commission of 30,000 rupees, which is 10 per cent of the 3,00,000 rupees left after it
visual.caption: Commission after charging = profit × rate ÷ (100 + rate)

slides.narration: A working partner may get a salary or commission, but only if the deed provides for it. Commission is often a percentage of net profit. If it is on profit before charging the commission, simply take the percentage. If it is on profit after charging the commission, divide by one hundred plus the rate. Ten per cent on rupees three lakh thirty thousand after charging gives rupees thirty thousand, exactly ten per cent of what is left.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a complete appropriation account
slides.body_md: **Saraswati Prints**, an imagined firm in Varanasi. Vikram, Leela and Yusuf share profits 3:2:2. Capitals ₹5,00,000, ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 6%; salary to Yusuf ₹36,000; commission to Leela 10% of net profit after charging it; transfer to general reserve ₹20,000; interest on drawings Vikram ₹3,000, Leela ₹2,000. Net profit before commission ₹3,30,000.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit)
To Vikram's Capital A/c (share of profit)
To Leela's Capital A/c (share of profit)
To Yusuf's Capital A/c (share of profit)

visual.alt: Profit and loss appropriation account of Saraswati Prints: net profit 3,30,000 and interest on drawings on the credit side; interest on capital, Yusuf's salary, Leela's commission 30,000, general reserve and shares of 81,000, 54,000 and 54,000 rupees on the debit side; both sides total 3,35,000
visual.caption: Divisible profit ₹1,89,000 shared 3:2:2.

slides.narration: Start with the net profit of rupees three lakh thirty thousand and add interest on drawings. Then debit interest on capital at six per cent, Yusuf's salary, Leela's commission of rupees thirty thousand and the transfer to reserve. The balance, rupees one lakh eighty nine thousand, is divided three to two to two: Vikram gets rupees eighty one thousand, and Leela and Yusuf get rupees fifty four thousand each. Equal totals on both sides are your check.

slides.heading: Quick check: commission after charging
slides.body_md: Use the after-charging formula.
slides.narration: Divide by one hundred plus the rate, not by one hundred. Then check that your answer is the rate on what is left.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Agreement to share the profit of a business run by all or any acting for all; 2 to 50 partners
Equal profits; no interest on capital or drawings; no salary; 6% a year on partners' loans
Fixed: capital and current accounts. Fluctuating: one capital account
Net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − commission − reserve = divisible profit
Appropriation: only out of profit, in the interest ratio if short. Charge: always

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the meaning of partnership, the rules when the deed is silent, the two capital methods, the appropriation account, interest on capital and drawings, and the commission formula

slides.narration: To sum up. A partnership rests on an agreement, best written as a deed; where the deed is silent, the Act applies. Capitals may be fixed, with current accounts, or fluctuating. The appropriation account starts from net profit, adds interest on drawings, and takes away interest on capital, salaries, commission and reserve before dividing the rest. Remember the average periods and the commission formula.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Read the deed first: is interest on capital an **appropriation** or a **charge**?
Interest on a partner's **loan** goes to the Profit and Loss Account, never the appropriation account.
Interest on additional capital runs **only from its date**: write the months.
Use the right average period; with no dates, use **6 months**.
Total both sides of every account before moving on.
slides.narration: Examiners give step marks, so show working notes for interest, commission and the divisible profit. The commonest mistakes are putting interest on a partner's loan in the appropriation account, charging interest on additional capital for the full year, and allowing interest on capital in a loss year when it is not a charge. Always total both sides of every account before you move on.

decks.title: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts — Part 2: Guarantee, Past Adjustments and Goodwill
goals: Account for a guarantee of minimum profit given by the firm or by particular partners, and for a guarantee given to the firm
Correct omissions and errors of a closed year with a single adjustment entry
Explain the nature of goodwill and the factors affecting it, and value it by the average profit, weighted average, super profit and capitalisation methods

slides.heading: Guarantee, past adjustments and goodwill
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **guarantee** of profit, **past adjustments**, and **goodwill**: its nature and its valuation.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: guarantee of profit, past adjustments, the nature of goodwill and the factors affecting it, and the methods of valuing goodwill
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part two we deal with three situations every partnership meets sooner or later. A new or junior partner may be promised a minimum profit. A mistake in last year's accounts may be found after the books are closed. And the partners may need to put a value on the reputation of their business, which accountants call goodwill. Let us take them one at a time.

slides.heading: Guarantee of minimum profit
bullets: Guarantee by the **firm**: all the other partners bear the deficiency in their mutual ratio.
Guarantee by **one partner**: that partner bears all of it.
Guarantee by **some partners** in an agreed ratio: they bear it in that ratio.

nodes.label: Divide profit in the normal ratio
Compare the guaranteed partner's share with the minimum
Deficiency borne by whoever gave the guarantee

visual.alt: Flow for a guarantee of minimum profit: divide the profit normally, compare the guaranteed partner's share with the minimum, find the deficiency, and charge it to whoever gave the guarantee
visual.caption: The firm's total profit never changes.

slides.narration: Sometimes a partner is promised that her share of profit will not fall below a fixed amount. First divide the profit in the normal ratio. If the guaranteed partner's share is below the minimum, the gap is the deficiency. Who fills it depends on who gave the guarantee: the firm, meaning all the other partners in their own ratio; one partner alone; or some partners in an agreed ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: guarantee by the firm
slides.body_md: **Konark Tiles**, an imagined firm in Puri. Dev, Esha and Pranav share profits 2:2:1. The **firm** guarantees Pranav a minimum profit of ₹60,000. Profit for 2025-26: ₹2,40,000.

rows: Deficiency borne by Dev and Esha 2:2

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: shares of 96,000, 96,000 and 48,000 rupees; Pranav's deficiency of 12,000 is borne equally by Dev and Esha, giving final shares of 90,000, 90,000 and 60,000 rupees

slides.narration: Pranav's normal share is one fifth of rupees two lakh forty thousand, that is rupees forty eight thousand. He was promised rupees sixty thousand, so the deficiency is rupees twelve thousand. As the firm gave the guarantee, Dev and Esha bear it in their own ratio, two to two, which is equal: rupees six thousand each. The final shares still add up to the same profit.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: guarantee by one partner
slides.body_md: Same firm and profit, but **Dev alone** gave the guarantee to Pranav.
bullets: Dev bears the whole deficiency of ₹12,000: final shares ₹84,000, ₹96,000 and ₹60,000.
Entry: Dev's Capital A/c Dr. ₹12,000; To Pranav's Capital A/c ₹12,000.

slides.narration: If Dev alone promised the minimum, he alone makes up the deficiency of rupees twelve thousand. Esha keeps her full rupees ninety six thousand, Dev is left with rupees eighty four thousand, and Pranav again gets rupees sixty thousand. The chart compares three cases: normal shares, a guarantee by the firm, and a guarantee by Dev alone. The total profit never changes; only its division does.

slides.body_md: Who gave the guarantee?
slides.narration: Find the guaranteed partner's normal share first, then decide who has to bear the gap.

slides.narration: A partner may instead guarantee that the firm itself will earn a minimum profit, perhaps because she brings in the customers. Suppose Esha guarantees the firm rupees two lakh seventy thousand. The actual profit is rupees two lakh forty thousand, so she brings in the shortfall of rupees thirty thousand, debited to her capital account. The full rupees two lakh seventy thousand is then divided in the usual ratio among all the partners, Esha included.

slides.heading: Past adjustments
bullets: Typical cases: interest on capital or drawings omitted, a salary omitted, profit shared in the wrong ratio.
Fixed capitals: use **current** accounts. Fluctuating capitals: use **capital** accounts.

nodes.label: Omission found after accounts are closed
Should have been credited or debited

visual.alt: Flow for a past adjustment: after the accounts are closed, list what each partner should have been credited or debited, subtract what was actually recorded, find the net effect which totals zero, and pass one adjustment entry
visual.caption: Closed accounts are never reopened.

slides.narration: Sometimes, after the books are closed, the partners find that interest on capital was left out, or that profit was shared in the wrong ratio. We do not reopen the accounts. Instead we draw up a table showing what each partner should have received, less what he actually received. The net effects always add up to zero, because the firm's profit has not changed. A single entry moves the difference.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: omitted interest
slides.body_md: **Godavari Traders**, an imagined firm in Nashik. Nisha, Tarun and Zoya share profits 2:2:1 with fixed capitals of ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000, ₹1,00,000. After the 2025-26 profit was distributed, they found that interest on capital at 10% and interest on drawings at 5% (drawings ₹40,000, ₹30,000, ₹20,000, dates unknown) were both omitted.

rows: Interest on drawings at 5% for 6 months (debit)
Net 57,750 taken back from profit in 2:2:1 (debit)

visual.alt: Past adjustment table for Nisha, Tarun and Zoya: interest on capital credited, interest on drawings debited, the net omission of 57,750 taken back in 2:2:1; net effect Nisha credit 5,900, Tarun debit 3,850, Zoya debit 2,050 rupees, totalling zero
visual.caption: The net effects add up to zero.

slides.narration: Credit each partner with the omitted interest on capital, and debit the omitted interest on drawings for six months at five per cent. The net omission of rupees fifty seven thousand seven hundred fifty has to come back out of the profit already shared, in the ratio two to two to one. Adding each column, Nisha gains rupees five thousand nine hundred, while Tarun and Zoya lose rupees three thousand eight hundred fifty and rupees two thousand fifty.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 (contd): the adjustment entry
slides.body_md: The net effects become **one** journal entry.
bullets: Debit the partners who **lose**; credit the partner who **gains**.
Capitals are fixed, so the **current** accounts are used.

rows: *(Being interest on capital and on drawings omitted, now adjusted)*

visual.alt: Journal entry: Tarun's current account debited 3,850 and Zoya's current account debited 2,050, Nisha's current account credited 5,900 rupees

slides.narration: The table becomes a single journal entry. Tarun's and Zoya's current accounts are debited with rupees three thousand eight hundred fifty and rupees two thousand fifty, and Nisha's current account is credited with rupees five thousand nine hundred. Because the capitals are fixed, current accounts are used. With fluctuating capitals the same amounts would go through the capital accounts.

slides.body_md: Interest omitted, less the same total taken back in the profit ratio.
slides.narration: Work out each partner's interest, take the total back in the profit-sharing ratio, and compare the two.

slides.heading: Goodwill: meaning and nature

rows: Value of the reputation that lets a business earn more than a normal profit
An intangible asset (not fictitious); cannot be sold apart from the business
Only purchased goodwill is recorded; self-generated goodwill never is
Change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement or death of a partner, sale of the business

visual.alt: Table on goodwill: its meaning as the value of reputation that earns above-normal profit, its nature as an intangible but real asset, the rule of Accounting Standard 26 that only purchased goodwill is recorded, and the occasions when it is valued

slides.narration: Customers return to a well-known sweet shop again and again. That pull, which lets a business earn more than an ordinary business, is goodwill. It is an intangible asset: it has real value but no physical form, and it cannot be sold apart from the business. Under Accounting Standard twenty six, only goodwill that has been paid for is recorded in the books.

slides.heading: Factors affecting goodwill

rows: the product is in steady demand
the business is on a busy, convenient site
costs are controlled and customers well served
it holds patents, licences or long contracts
it is long established and well known

visual.alt: Table of factors affecting goodwill: nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages such as patents and licences, and the period in business

slides.narration: What makes goodwill high or low? Anything that changes the profits a firm can expect. A product in steady demand, a busy location, efficient management, little competition, and special advantages such as patents, licences or long contracts all raise goodwill. An old, well-known name helps too. Move the same shop to a quiet lane, and its goodwill falls.

slides.heading: Quick check: what lowers goodwill?
slides.body_md: Think about future profits.
slides.narration: Ask which change would bring fewer customers or lower profits in the future.

slides.heading: Methods of valuing goodwill
bullets: **Normal profit** = capital employed × normal rate of return ÷ 100.
**Capital employed** = assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − outside liabilities.
Use **normal** profits: add back abnormal losses, remove one-time gains.

nodes.label: Average profit: average profit × years' purchase
Weighted average profit: more weight to recent years
Super profit: (average − normal profit) × years' purchase
Capitalisation: of average profit or of super profit

visual.alt: Flow of the four methods of valuing goodwill: average profit times years of purchase, weighted average profit, super profit times years of purchase, and capitalisation of average or super profit
visual.caption: Normal profit = capital employed × normal rate ÷ 100

slides.narration: Your syllabus has four methods. The average profit method multiplies average profit by a number of years' purchase. The weighted average method gives more weight to recent years. The super profit method values only the profit earned above the normal profit. The capitalisation methods ask what capital would earn the firm's profit at the normal rate of return.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: average and weighted average profit
slides.body_md: **Malabar Boatworks**, an imagined firm in Kozhikode. Profits: 2022-23 ₹1,60,000; 2023-24 ₹1,90,000; 2024-25 ₹1,40,000; 2025-26 ₹2,10,000 (2024-25 after an abnormal flood loss of ₹30,000). Goodwill at 3 years' purchase.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 4: normal profits 1,60,000, 1,90,000, 1,70,000, 2,10,000 rupees total 7,30,000, average 1,82,500; with weights 1 to 4 the products total 18,90,000, weighted average 1,89,000 rupees
visual.caption: Simple average ₹1,82,500 → goodwill ₹5,47,500; weighted average ₹1,89,000 → goodwill ₹5,67,000 (3 years' purchase).

slides.narration: First make each year normal. The flood loss of rupees thirty thousand will not recur, so add it back. The four normal profits average rupees one lakh eighty two thousand five hundred, so at three years' purchase goodwill is rupees five lakh forty seven thousand five hundred. With weights one to four, the weighted average is rupees one lakh eighty nine thousand, giving goodwill of rupees five lakh sixty seven thousand. Rising profits push the weighted figure higher.

slides.heading: Simple and weighted average compared

visual.alt: Bar chart of normal profits of 160, 190, 170, 210 thousand rupees over four years, with a dashed line at the simple average of 182.5 and a solid line at the weighted average of 189 thousand
visual.caption: With rising profits, the weighted average sits above the simple average.

slides.narration: The bars show the four normal profits, rising over time. The dashed line is the simple average and the solid line the weighted average. Because recent years carry more weight, the weighted average sits closer to the latest profits. That is why a firm whose profits show a clear trend prefers the weighted average method.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: super profit method
slides.body_md: Same firm. Assets other than goodwill ₹13,50,000; outside liabilities ₹3,50,000; normal rate of return 12.5%; average profit ₹1,82,500. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profit.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 5: capital employed 10,00,000, normal profit 1,25,000, super profit 57,500 and goodwill 1,72,500 rupees

slides.narration: Capital employed is assets other than goodwill less outside liabilities: rupees ten lakh. A normal firm would earn twelve and a half per cent on it, which is rupees one lakh twenty five thousand. Our firm earns rupees one lakh eighty two thousand five hundred, so its super profit is rupees fifty seven thousand five hundred. Three years' purchase of the super profit gives goodwill of rupees one lakh seventy two thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: capitalisation methods
slides.body_md: Same firm and figures. Value goodwill by capitalising (a) the average profit, (b) the super profit.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 6: capitalised value 14,60,000 less capital employed 10,00,000 gives goodwill 4,60,000; capitalising the super profit of 57,500 gives the same 4,60,000 rupees
visual.caption: Same figures, same goodwill: the two formulas are one formula rearranged.

slides.narration: Capitalising the average profit asks what capital would earn rupees one lakh eighty two thousand five hundred at twelve and a half per cent: rupees fourteen lakh sixty thousand. Subtract the capital actually employed, rupees ten lakh, and goodwill is rupees four lakh sixty thousand. Capitalising the super profit at the same rate gives the same rupees four lakh sixty thousand. The two methods are one formula written two ways.

slides.heading: Quick check: super profit
slides.body_md: Normal profit first, then super profit, then years' purchase.
slides.narration: Follow the three steps of the last worked example, in the same order.

rows: Deficiency borne by the other partners in their mutual ratio
That partner bears the whole deficiency
Guarantor brings in the shortfall; the full guaranteed profit is divided
Should-be minus actual for each partner; net effect zero; one entry
Intangible; only purchased goodwill is recorded (Accounting Standard 26)
Average profit × 100 ÷ rate − capital employed = super profit × 100 ÷ rate

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: who bears a deficiency under each kind of guarantee, the rule for past adjustments, the nature of goodwill and the formulas of the four valuation methods

slides.narration: To sum up. A deficiency under a guarantee is borne by whoever gave it, and the firm's total profit never changes. Past errors are corrected with one entry, built from a table whose net effect is zero. Goodwill is an intangible asset, recorded only when purchased. We value it from normal profits by the average, weighted average, super profit and capitalisation methods.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In guarantee questions, state **who** gave the guarantee before dividing the deficiency.
In past adjustments, total the net row: it **must be zero**.
Normalise profits first: add back abnormal losses, remove one-time gains, deduct a fair salary for unpaid partner work.
Keep existing goodwill and fictitious assets **out** of capital employed.
Write the years' purchase and the rate in every goodwill working.
slides.narration: In the exam, read the guarantee clause twice, because the guarantor decides who bears the deficiency. In past adjustments, the net effects must total zero; if they do not, recheck your table. For goodwill, normalise each year's profit first, keep existing goodwill out of capital employed, and show every step: average profit, normal profit, super profit and the final value.

sections.heading: 2. Partners' capital accounts: fixed and fluctuating
sections.body_md:
**Fixed capital method:** two accounts per partner.
- **Capital account**: opening capital, additional capital (credit), capital permanently withdrawn (debit). Always a credit balance.
- **Current account**: interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit (credit); drawings, interest on drawings, share of loss (debit). May have a debit balance.

**Fluctuating capital method:** one capital account per partner records all these items; its balance changes every year. Use it when a question names no method.

**Finding opening capital from closing capital:** closing capital + drawings + interest on drawings + share of loss − share of profit − interest on capital − salary − commission − additional capital = opening capital.

key_terms.definition_md: Shows only capital brought in or permanently withdrawn.
Records the routine credits and debits of a partner under the fixed capital method.
A capital account that records every adjustment, so its balance changes each year.

rows: Same unless capital is added or permanently withdrawn
Possible in the current account only

sections.heading: 4. Interest on drawings, salary and commission
sections.body_md:
**Interest on drawings** is charged only if the deed provides; it is credited to the appropriation account and debited to the partner.

- Equal amounts at regular intervals: interest = total drawings × rate ÷ 100 × average period ÷ 12.
- Average period: monthly 6½ / 6 / 5½ months (beginning / middle / end); quarterly 7½ / 6 / 4½; half-yearly 9 / 6 / 3.
- Dates not given: 6 months.
- Unequal amounts or dates (**product method**): multiply each amount by the months left to the year end, add the products, and charge interest for one month on the total.

**Salary and commission** to partners are appropriations, payable only if the deed provides.
- Commission on profit **before** charging it = profit × rate ÷ 100.
- Commission on profit **after** charging it = profit × rate ÷ (100 + rate).

key_terms.definition_md: The average number of months for which equal drawings remain with the partner.
Interest on drawings worked out from the sum of each amount multiplied by the months it was outstanding.

sections.heading: 5. Guarantee of profit
sections.body_md:
**Guarantee to a partner:** a partner is promised a minimum share. Divide the profit normally; if the share is below the minimum, the **deficiency** is borne by:
- the **firm**: all other partners in their mutual profit-sharing ratio;
- **one partner**: that partner alone;
- **some partners**: in the ratio they agreed.

In the appropriation account the guaranteed partner is shown with the minimum and the guarantors with their reduced shares (or the deficiency is passed by an entry: guarantor's capital Dr., to guaranteed partner's capital).

**Guarantee to the firm:** a partner promises that the firm will earn at least a stated profit. The shortfall is brought in by that partner (debited to his capital, credited to the appropriation account) and the full guaranteed profit is divided among all partners.

The firm's total profit is never changed by a guarantee to a partner.

sections.heading: 6. Past adjustments
sections.body_md:
Errors or omissions found **after** the accounts are closed (interest on capital or drawings, salary, commission, wrong profit-sharing ratio) are corrected without reopening the accounts.

**Method:**
1. For each partner, list what should have been credited (+) or debited (−).
2. Deduct what was actually credited (reverse the profit wrongly shared).
3. Find the **net effect**; the net effects of all partners total **zero**.
4. Pass one entry: debit the partners who lose, credit those who gain (current accounts if capitals are fixed, capital accounts if fluctuating).

If only an appropriation such as interest on capital is omitted, the same total is taken back from the partners in the profit-sharing ratio.

sections.heading: 7. Goodwill: nature, factors and valuation
sections.body_md:
**Goodwill** is the value of a firm's reputation that lets it earn more than a normal profit. It is an **intangible** asset (not fictitious) and cannot be sold apart from the business. Under **Accounting Standard 26**, only purchased goodwill is recorded.

**Factors:** nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages (patents, licences, contracts), period in business.

**Valuation** (use normal profits: add back abnormal losses, remove non-recurring gains, deduct a fair salary for unpaid partner work):
- **Average profit:** goodwill = average profit × number of years' purchase.
- **Weighted average profit:** weighted average = sum of (profit × weight) ÷ sum of weights; × years' purchase.
- **Super profit:** normal profit = capital employed × normal rate ÷ 100; super profit = average profit − normal profit; goodwill = super profit × years' purchase.
- **Capitalisation of average profit:** capitalised value = average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate; goodwill = capitalised value − capital employed.
- **Capitalisation of super profit:** goodwill = super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate.

**Capital employed** = total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − outside liabilities.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split**
- 1 mark: one correct option or term.
- 3 marks: a short computation with its working (for example interest on drawings, an adjustment entry or a goodwill value).
- 4 marks: a full appropriation account, a guarantee or a goodwill problem with every step.
- 6 marks: capital or current accounts with the appropriation account, or a multi-error past adjustment.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting interest on a partner's loan in the appropriation account (it is a charge).
- Allowing interest on capital in a loss year when the deed does not call it a charge.
- Charging interest on additional capital for the whole year.
- Using the wrong average period, or forgetting 6 months when dates are not given.
- Calculating commission on profit before charging it when the deed says after charging.
- Letting the guaranteed partner bear part of his own deficiency.
- A past-adjustment table whose net effects do not total zero.
- Including goodwill already in the books in capital employed.

All firms and figures in SOYL practice are imagined; the board paper will give its own.

cards.front_md: **Partnership** (Indian Partnership Act, 1932)
cards.back_md: A relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business run by all or any of them acting for all.

cards.front_md: Minimum and maximum number of partners
cards.back_md: At least **2**; at most **50** (Companies Act, 2013 and its rules).

cards.front_md: **Mutual agency**
cards.back_md: Each partner is an agent of the firm and of the others, and also a principal.

cards.front_md: Is a written deed compulsory?
cards.back_md: **No.** The agreement may be oral; a written, stamped deed is advisable.

cards.front_md: Deed silent: sharing of profit
cards.back_md: **Equally**, whatever the capitals.

cards.front_md: Deed silent: interest on capital and drawings
cards.back_md: **None** allowed on capital; **none** charged on drawings.

cards.front_md: Deed silent: salary to a working partner
cards.back_md: **Not allowed**.

cards.front_md: Deed silent: interest on a partner's loan
cards.back_md: **6% per annum**, a charge against profit.

cards.front_md: **Fixed capital method**
cards.back_md: Capital account (permanent changes only) + current account (all routine items).

cards.front_md: **Fluctuating capital method**
cards.back_md: One capital account records every adjustment; balance changes yearly. Default method.

cards.front_md: Can a current account have a debit balance?
cards.back_md: **Yes**, when debits (drawings, interest on drawings, loss) exceed credits.

cards.front_md: Charge or appropriation: interest on a partner's loan
cards.back_md: **Charge**: Profit and Loss Account.

cards.front_md: Charge or appropriation: partner's salary
cards.back_md: **Appropriation**: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

cards.front_md: **Divisible profit**
cards.back_md: Net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − commission − reserve.

cards.front_md: Profit less than interest on capital (appropriation)
cards.back_md: Whole profit shared in the **ratio of interest due**.

cards.front_md: Loss year, interest on capital not a charge
cards.back_md: **No interest** on capital.

cards.front_md: Interest on additional capital
cards.back_md: From the **date it was brought in** to the year end.

cards.front_md: Average period: monthly drawings (beginning / middle / end)
cards.back_md: **6½ / 6 / 5½** months.

cards.front_md: Average period: quarterly drawings (beginning / middle / end)
cards.back_md: **7½ / 6 / 4½** months.

cards.front_md: Interest on drawings when dates are not given
cards.back_md: For **6 months** on the total.

cards.front_md: Commission after charging such commission
cards.back_md: Profit × rate ÷ **(100 + rate)**.

cards.front_md: Guarantee by the firm: who bears the deficiency?
cards.back_md: The **other partners** in their mutual profit-sharing ratio.

cards.front_md: Guarantee by one partner: who bears the deficiency?
cards.back_md: **That partner alone**.

cards.front_md: Guarantee to the firm by a partner
cards.back_md: The partner brings in the shortfall; the guaranteed profit is divided among all.

cards.front_md: Past adjustment: net effect of all partners
cards.back_md: Always **zero**; one entry debits losers and credits gainers.

cards.front_md: **Goodwill**
cards.back_md: Value of reputation that enables a business to earn above-normal profit; an intangible asset.

cards.front_md: Accounting Standard 26 on goodwill
cards.back_md: Only **purchased** goodwill is recorded; self-generated goodwill is not.

cards.front_md: **Super profit**
cards.back_md: Average profit − normal profit (capital employed × normal rate ÷ 100).

cards.front_md: Capitalisation of average profit
cards.back_md: Average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate − capital employed.

cards.front_md: Capitalisation of super profit
cards.back_md: Super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate (same answer as the other capitalisation method).

cards.front_md: **Capital employed**
cards.back_md: Assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − outside liabilities.

cards.front_md: Abnormal loss in a past year's profit
cards.back_md: **Add it back** before averaging; remove one-time gains.

questions.stem_md: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 says that the business of a firm may be carried on by all the partners **or by any of them acting for all**. This part of the definition is the basis of which feature of partnership?

options.text_md: Unlimited liability
Mutual agency
Sharing of profits
Voluntary registration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Mutual agency. A partner who acts for all binds the others, so every partner is both an agent and a principal of the firm. Unlimited liability and profit sharing are separate features, and registration is not part of the definition.

questions.stem_md: Under the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014, the **maximum** number of partners a partnership firm may have is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 50. Rule 10 of the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 caps a firm at 50 partners; the minimum is two.

questions.stem_md: There is no partnership deed. Partner Devika lends ₹1,00,000 to the firm, over and above her capital. Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 she is entitled to interest on this loan at

options.text_md: 6% per annum, charged to the Profit and Loss Account
6% per annum, paid only out of profits
12% per annum, charged to the Profit and Loss Account
nothing, because there is no deed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 6% per annum, charged to the Profit and Loss Account. When partners have not agreed otherwise, the Act allows 6% a year on a loan or advance by a partner. It is a charge, so it is paid even in a year of loss.

questions.stem_md: Farid invested ₹6,00,000 and Gauri ₹2,00,000 in an imagined travel agency in Kochi. They never agreed how profits would be shared. A profit of ₹1,60,000 for the year will be shared as

options.text_md: ₹1,20,000 to Farid and ₹40,000 to Gauri, in the capital ratio
₹1,60,000 to Farid, as the larger investor
₹80,000 to each partner
whatever ratio the firm's auditor decides

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹80,000 to each partner. Without an agreement the Act requires profits and losses to be shared equally, whatever the capitals contributed.

questions.stem_md: Kavya and Ruhi run an imagined design studio in Indore without a partnership deed. Kavya works full time; Ruhi comes in only at weekends. Kavya claims a salary of ₹20,000 per month. Under the Act, Kavya

options.text_md: gets ₹20,000 per month, because she works full time
gets a salary, but only out of profits
gets no salary, because a partner is not entitled to remuneration without an agreement
gets half the salary she claims, because Ruhi also works

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** gets no salary, because a partner is not entitled to remuneration without an agreement. The Act gives no salary or commission to a partner for taking part in the business unless the partners agree to pay it, however unequal their work.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the absence of a partnership deed, a partner who has lent money to the firm receives interest at 6% per annum even in a year when the firm makes a loss.

**Reason (R):** Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profits and is debited to the Profit and Loss Account.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true. Because the interest is a charge (an expense of the firm), it is payable whatever the result of the year, which is exactly why A holds.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A partnership deed must be in writing; an oral agreement between partners is not valid.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The agreement may be oral or written. A written and stamped deed is advisable because it settles disputes, but the Act does not make writing compulsory.

questions.stem_md: Every partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners, and also a principal. This feature of partnership is called ___ agency.
questions.solution_md: It is mutual agency: an act of one partner in the course of business binds the firm and all partners.

questions.stem_md: There is no partnership deed. Match each item with the rule of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 that applies to it.

options.text_md: Interest on partners' capitals
Interest on partners' drawings
Interest on a loan given by a partner
Sharing of profits and losses

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). When the deed is silent: no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, 6% a year on partners' loans, and equal sharing of profits and losses.

questions.stem_md: Hari, Jaya and Kiran run an imagined furniture firm in Jodhpur and have **no partnership deed**. Their capitals are ₹6,00,000, ₹3,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. Kiran also lent the firm ₹80,000 on 1 October 2025. At the year end (31 March 2026) three claims are made: (i) Hari wants profits shared in the capital ratio; (ii) Jaya, who works full time, wants a salary of ₹15,000 per month; (iii) Kiran wants interest at 12% per annum on her loan. Settle each claim, giving reasons.
questions.solution_md: Apply the three default rules of the Act; the loan earns interest only from the date it was given.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Profit sharing:** Hari's claim is not valid. Without a deed, profits are shared **equally** among Hari, Jaya and Kiran, whatever their capitals.
2. **Salary:** Jaya's claim is not valid. The Act allows **no salary or commission** to a partner unless all partners agree to it.
3. **Interest on loan:** Kiran gets interest at **6% per annum**, not 12%: ₹80,000 × 6/100 × 6/12 = **₹2,400** for 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026. It is a **charge**, debited to the Profit and Loss Account and payable even if there is a loss.

marking_scheme.step: Interest at 6% for 6 months = ₹2,400 as a charge

questions.stem_md: State any **six** matters that a partnership deed usually covers.
questions.solution_md: Any six points from the list earn half a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Name and address of the firm and of every partner, and the nature of the business.
2. Date of commencement and duration of the partnership.
3. Capital contributed by each partner.
4. Profit-sharing ratio.
5. Interest on capital and on drawings, and the rate of interest on partners' loans.
6. Salary or commission payable to partners.
7. Rules for admission, retirement or death of a partner, valuation of goodwill, settlement of disputes and dissolution.

marking_scheme.step: Any six correct matters, ½ mark each

questions.stem_md: Sisters Ritika and Sonal start an imagined bakery in Shillong as partners. Using their business as the example, explain any **four** features of a partnership.
questions.solution_md: Each feature needs its meaning and a link to the bakery; any four of the six.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Two or more persons:** Ritika and Sonal are two; a firm may have at most 50 partners.
2. **Agreement:** they are partners because they agreed, orally or in writing, not because they are sisters.
3. **Lawful business:** the agreement is to carry on a business, here baking and selling bread and cakes.
4. **Sharing of profits:** they share the profits and losses of the bakery in an agreed ratio.
5. **Mutual agency:** either sister may act for both; an order Sonal places for flour binds Ritika too.
6. **Unlimited liability:** if the bakery cannot pay its debts, creditors can recover them from either sister's private assets.

questions.stem_md: Under the **fixed capital method**, which item is recorded in a partner's capital account rather than in the current account?

options.text_md: Additional capital introduced by the partner
Interest on capital for the year
Share of profit for the year
Drawings made during the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Additional capital introduced by the partner. Only permanent changes in capital, such as fresh capital brought in or capital permanently withdrawn, pass through the capital account; the routine items of the year go to the current account.

questions.stem_md: If a question does not say which method to use, the partners' capital accounts are prepared by the

options.text_md: fixed capital method
average capital method
net worth method
fluctuating capital method

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** fluctuating capital method. In the absence of an instruction, capitals are taken as fluctuating: every adjustment is recorded in the capital account itself.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under the fixed capital method, a partner's **current account** can show a debit balance.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** If drawings, interest on drawings and a share of loss exceed the credits of the year, the current account goes into debit, while the capital account keeps its credit balance.

questions.stem_md: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's capital account normally shows a ___ balance.
questions.solution_md: It always shows a credit balance, because only capital brought in or permanently withdrawn passes through it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm keeps its partners' capitals **fixed**. Match each item with the place where it is recorded.

options.text_md: Additional capital brought in
Capital permanently withdrawn
Salary allowed to a partner
Interest charged on drawings

match_right.text_md: Debit side of the current account
Credit side of the capital account
Credit side of the current account
Debit side of the capital account

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Permanent changes go to the capital account; salary (a credit to the partner) and interest on drawings (a debit) go to the current account.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the fixed capital method, interest on drawings is debited to the partner's capital account.

**Reason (R):** Under the fixed capital method, the routine items of the year, such as drawings, interest and share of profit, pass through the partners' current accounts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: interest on drawings is a routine item, so it is debited to the current account. R is true and states the rule correctly.

During 2025-26 she withdrew ₹48,000, her share of profit of ₹90,000 was credited, and she brought in additional capital of ₹50,000 on 1 October 2025. Calculate her capital on 1 April 2025 and the interest on her capital at 8% per annum.
questions.solution_md: Reverse every change of the year to reach the opening figure, then charge interest on the opening capital for the full year and on the addition from its date.

| Particulars | ₹ |

| Add: Drawings during the year | 48,000 |

| Less: Additional capital brought in on 1 October 2025 | 50,000 |

- On ₹3,70,000 for 12 months: ₹3,70,000 × 8/100 = ₹29,600

- On ₹50,000 for 6 months (1 October to 31 March): ₹50,000 × 8/100 × 6/12 = ₹2,000

- **Total interest on capital = ₹31,600**

questions.stem_md: As per Accounting Standard 26, goodwill is recorded in the books of a firm only when

options.text_md: consideration in money or money's worth has been paid for it
all the partners agree on its value
the firm has earned profits for at least three years
a registered valuer certifies its value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** consideration in money or money's worth has been paid for it. Only purchased goodwill is recorded; goodwill generated inside the business is never brought into the books.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following would most likely **reduce** the goodwill of an imagined sweet shop?

options.text_md: A long-term contract to supply sweets to a large hotel
Moving the shop from a busy market to a quiet back lane
An experienced and well-liked head cook
A popular recipe that only this shop can make

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Moving the shop from a busy market to a quiet back lane. Location affects how many customers come in; a move to a quiet lane cuts expected future profits. The other three would raise goodwill.

questions.stem_md: The goodwill of a business is

options.text_md: a fictitious asset, like a debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account
a current asset that can be sold separately at any time
a liability of the firm towards its partners
an intangible asset that can be sold only along with the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an intangible asset that can be sold only along with the business. Goodwill has real value (buyers pay for it) but no physical form, and it cannot be separated from the business.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm employs capital of ₹7,50,000. The normal rate of return in its industry is 12%. Its normal profit is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹90,000. Normal profit = capital employed × normal rate ÷ 100 = ₹7,50,000 × 12/100.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm's profits were ₹1,20,000 in 2023-24, ₹1,50,000 in 2024-25 and ₹1,80,000 in 2025-26. Using weights 1, 2 and 3 respectively, the weighted average profit is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹1,60,000. Products: 1,20,000 + 3,00,000 + 5,40,000 = 9,60,000; divided by the sum of weights 6.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bakery in Ooty earned profits of ₹1,00,000, ₹1,30,000, ₹1,60,000 in the last three years. Calculate its goodwill at **two years' purchase** of the average profit (in ₹).
An imagined courier firm employs capital of ₹8,00,000; the normal rate of return is 10%. Its average profit is ₹1,10,000. Find goodwill at **three years' purchase of super profit** (in ₹).
The super profit of an imagined software firm is ₹24,000 a year and the normal rate of return is 12%. Value its goodwill by **capitalising the super profit** (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Goodwill = super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate = 24,000 × 100/12 = ₹2,00,000.

questions.stem_md: For valuing goodwill, capital employed = total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − ___.
questions.solution_md: Capital employed is the total of real assets less outside liabilities such as creditors, bills payable and loans.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Given the same average profit, capital employed and normal rate of return, capitalising the average profit and capitalising the super profit give the **same** value of goodwill.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Super profit × 100 ÷ rate = (average profit − capital employed × rate ÷ 100) × 100 ÷ rate = average profit × 100 ÷ rate − capital employed, which is exactly the other method's result.

questions.stem_md: Match each method of valuing goodwill with its formula.

options.text_md: Average profit method
Super profit method
Capitalisation of average profit
Capitalisation of super profit

match_right.text_md: Super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate of return
(Average profit − normal profit) × number of years' purchase
Average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate − capital employed
Average profit × number of years' purchase

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The first two multiply by years' purchase; the capitalisation methods divide by the normal rate of return.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Goodwill is an intangible asset.

**Reason (R):** Goodwill is a fictitious asset, like discount on the issue of debentures.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: a fictitious asset has no realisable value, whereas goodwill can be sold with the business and has a real value.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Abnormal losses are added back to a year's profit before the average profit is calculated for valuing goodwill.

**Reason (R):** As per Accounting Standard 26, self-generated goodwill is not recorded in the books.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. A is about using normal, repeatable profits; R is about recording goodwill in the books, so it does not explain A.

questions.stem_md: Explain any **three** factors that affect the value of a firm's goodwill, with one example each.
questions.solution_md: Any three factors that change expected future profits, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Location:** a shop on a busy road draws more customers and earns more, so its goodwill is higher; a chemist next to a hospital is an example.
2. **Efficiency of management:** able managers keep costs low and profits high, for example a well-run restaurant with little waste.
3. **Special advantages:** a patent, a licence or a long supply contract, such as an exclusive contract with a railway canteen, raises expected profits.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bicycle-parts firm in Ludhiana earned profits of ₹90,000, ₹1,10,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,50,000 in 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26. Profits are rising steadily, so the partners agree to value goodwill at **two years' purchase of the weighted average profit**, using weights 1, 2, 3 and 4. Calculate the goodwill.
questions.solution_md: Weights give recent years more say when profits show a trend.

questions.stem_md: The partners of an imagined tailoring firm in Lucknow agree to value goodwill at **two and a half years' purchase** of the average profit of the last five years. Profits were: 2021-22 ₹1,20,000; 2022-23 ₹1,50,000, which included a one-time gain of ₹30,000 on selling an old delivery van; 2023-24 ₹90,000, after a loss of ₹40,000 from a fire in the store; 2024-25 ₹1,60,000; 2025-26 ₹1,70,000. One partner manages the firm without a salary; a fair salary for this work would be ₹12,000 a year. Calculate the goodwill.
questions.solution_md: Goodwill rests on profits expected to recur, so remove one-time items and charge a fair reward for the partner's work before averaging.

marking_scheme.step: Non-recurring gain deducted and abnormal loss added back

questions.stem_md: The balance sheet of an imagined coaching centre in Kota shows total assets of ₹9,40,000, including goodwill of ₹40,000, and outside liabilities of creditors ₹1,20,000 and a bank loan of ₹1,80,000. Its profits for the last three years were ₹95,000, ₹1,02,000, ₹1,09,000. The normal rate of return is 12%. Value its goodwill at **three years' purchase of super profit**.
questions.solution_md: Existing goodwill is left out of capital employed; super profit is the excess of average over normal profit.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bus-body building firm in Belagavi has these assets: land and building ₹6,00,000, machinery ₹3,50,000, stock ₹1,40,000, debtors ₹1,10,000, cash ₹40,000, and goodwill ₹50,000. Its liabilities to outsiders are: creditors ₹1,60,000, bills payable ₹40,000, bank loan ₹2,00,000. Profits of the last three years were ₹1,30,000, ₹1,42,000, ₹1,51,000, and the normal rate of return is 15%. (a) Calculate the capital employed. (b) Value goodwill by capitalising the average profit. (c) Value goodwill by capitalising the super profit. (d) Explain why (b) and (c) agree.
questions.solution_md: Compute capital employed once and use it in both methods; the algebra of the two formulas shows why they agree.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Capital employed = assets other than goodwill ₹12,40,000 − outside liabilities ₹4,00,000 = **₹8,40,000** (goodwill already in the books is left out).

**(b)** Average profit = (1,30,000 + 1,42,000 + 1,51,000) ÷ 3 = ₹1,41,000. Capitalised value = ₹1,41,000 × 100/15 = ₹9,40,000. Goodwill = ₹9,40,000 − ₹8,40,000 = **₹1,00,000**.

**(c)** Normal profit = ₹8,40,000 × 15/100 = ₹1,26,000; super profit = ₹1,41,000 − ₹1,26,000 = ₹15,000. Goodwill = ₹15,000 × 100/15 = **₹1,00,000**.

**(d)** Capitalising the super profit gives (average profit − capital employed × rate ÷ 100) × 100 ÷ rate, which simplifies to average profit × 100 ÷ rate − capital employed: the formula of (b). With the same figures the two methods must give the same goodwill.
